newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia coffee steady, London seen rising.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia coffee steady, London seen rising.

text.p: Indonesian Robusta coffee prices edged up on Thursday, with sentiment boosted by a fresh surge in London futures overnight, traders said.

They said the local price was quoted at 3,200 rupiah/kg in Lampung, capital of the key growing region of South Sumatra, up from 3,100 rupiah from Wednesday. The export price was quoted at $1,400/tonne FOB Lampung, up from $1,390-$1,400.
The traders said they expected London's benchmark May contract to open higher later on Thursday by $20-$30.
"The local market got a boost from London, despite prices there weakening towards the close," one trader said. "I see London prices opening $20-$30 higher today."
London futures retreated slightly from a fresh surge on Wednesday as some speculators who had bought ahead of the opening of the New York market sold back.
Fund and trade buying took the front-month May to its intra-day peak of $1,650 a tonne, the highest in two weeks, after news of a smaller-than-expected rise in the U.S. green coffee stocks.

The Green Coffee Association of New York reported coffee stocks in U.S. warehouses rose by a modest 111,000 60-kg bags to 1.65 million in March. It was well below market expectations of a 200,000 to 300,000 bag increase.
The news sparked a rally in New York, where May delivery coffee rose 15.65 cents to close at 208.05 cents a pound, the highest price for coffee since September 1994.

Traders in Indonesia said the local market was active, with buyers covering positions. "Exporters have been buying...and are covering shorts," one trader said. He said some 70,000 tonnes of beans have already been committed.
The trader said supply was expected to get tight towards the end of the year due to a shortfall in production this year, adding that exporters were beginning to accept the output drop.
"The exporters have already adapted to the lower crop expectations. Two months ago, we had very wide differentials but I don't see it anymore," he said.

He said supply was expected to get tight towards the end of the year. "It's going to be a bit tricky from September onwards," he said, adding that during a recent trip to Lampung he found the coffee trees there to be in poor shape.
"The famers were telling me that the flowering process had been affected by strong winds," he said.

Oesman Soedargo, chairman of the Association of Indonesian Coffee Exporters, said last Monday the country's production was expected to fall by some 30 percent this year from an original forecast of 480,000 tonnes due to bad weather. He said the total exportable volume would amount to 220,000 tonnes.
Another trader said he expected production to be down by not more than 20 percent, adding that supply remained ample.
"I figure the decline would not exceed 20 percent. But the effect of the drop has yet to be felt," he said.
Traders said there had been indications from key Asian Robusta producer Vietnam that it would sell leftover coffee.
"I don't know exactly what the number is but I hear that Vietnam might have up to 30,000 tonnes of leftover coffee to sell," one said.
